description: Table 1 is a single-image, four-column reference table (no plots, spectra or micrographs) summarising how seven alloying/microalloying elements act in austenitic Fe–Mn–Al–C steels. Column headers read "Element", "κ-carbide behavior", "Effect on microstructure" and "Mechanical properties>" (the trailing ">" is printed in the header cell). The seven rows are Si, Cr, Cu, V, Nb, Mo and Ni, each giving a prose entry. Si promotes intragranular κ-carbide formation, accelerates nucleation, increases carbon partitioning, refines grain structure and raises yield strength up to 950 MPa while slightly reducing elongation. Cr suppresses intergranular κ-carbides, promotes fine intragranular ones, delays precipitation at low content, stabilises austenite, suppresses DO3 and improves oxidation resistance. Cu enhances κ-carbide precipitation with Cu-rich clusters, promotes a Cu-B2 phase and gives 808 MPa with 20%–40% ductility. V binds carbon, precipitates VC plus κ-carbides, reaching >1300 MPa with ~41% ductility. Nb forms NbC competing with κ-carbides, giving UTS >900 MPa and ≈6% elongation gain. Mo partially substitutes κ-carbides with Mo₂C (680 MPa, hardness). Ni reduces κ-carbide size, co-precipitates NiAl (B2), promotes δ-ferrite, reaching >1300 MPa with 22%–27% elongation.

observations.observation: The table is organised into four columns headed 'Element', 'κ-carbide behavior', 'Effect on microstructure' and 'Mechanical properties>' — the final header cell is printed with a stray '>' character.
The rows enumerate exactly seven elements: Si, Cr, Cu, V, Nb, Mo and Ni.
The Si row states it 'Increases yield strength (up to 950 MPa), reduces elongation slightly' and that excessive Si may promote intergranular κ-carbides and risk a red scale defect.

The Cr row states it suppresses intergranular κ-carbides, promotes fine intragranular κ-carbides, delays precipitation at low content, refines grains, stabilises austenite and suppresses DO3 at moderate content.
The Cu row reports 'Improves strength (808 MPa) and ductility (20%–40%) via dual strengthening' and promotes a Cu-B2 phase.
The V row reports strength increased 'to >1300 MPa' and ductility enhanced to '~41%', with dual precipitation of VC and κ-carbides.
The Nb row reports 'Enhances strength (UTS >900 MPa), improves elongation by ≈6%', attributed to NbC precipitates competing with κ-carbides.
The Mo row reports 'Increases strength (680 MPa), hardness; slight ductility loss at high content' and partial substitution of κ-carbides by Mo₂C.
The Ni row reports 'Strength >1300 MPa, elongation 22%–27%; enhances creep resistance', with co-precipitation of NiAl (B2) and κ-carbides and promotion of δ-ferrite.
Precipitates and phases named across the table are κ-carbide, VC, NbC, Mo₂C, NiAl (B2), Cu-B2, DO3 and δ-ferrite.
The caption states the table shows the effect of alloying and microalloying elements on Fe–Mn–Al–C steels.

The citing text states the table provides a comparative overview of how Si, Cr, Cu, V, Nb, Mo and Ni influence microstructure, κ-carbide precipitation and mechanical properties, consolidating findings from various studies as a reference for alloy design and processing optimisation of lightweight high-strength steels.
The table contains no plotted data, error bars or measured curves; all quantitative values appear only as numbers embedded in the prose cells.
